facts.name: Little Bluestem
facts.notes: An upright prairie grass with blue-green blades that turn copper-red in fall and stand up all winter.

sources.title: Michigan Wildflower Farm: Dryland species list
sources.note: Michigan seed grower; marks any species that is not native to Michigan.

companions.why: Pair with dark-leaved Heuchera; combine with aster, tall sedums like 'Autumn Joy', yarrow, rudbeckias and purple coneflower.

sources.title: Purdue Extension: Gardening with Bulbs

companions.why: Combines well with purple coneflower, bee balm and native grasses; in gardens with Japanese anemones.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Anise Hyssop article

companions.why: Combines with yellow flowers such as coreopsis and goldenrod, pink ones such as purple coneflower, prairie grasses and silver plants such as Stachys (lamb's ear).

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Blazing Star article

companions.why: Combine with Penstemon 'Husker Red' or purple speedwells; works well with coreopsis, purple coneflower, blazing star, black-eyed Susan, little bluestem and prairie dropseed.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Butterfly Weed article

companions.why: Purdue Extension: interplant daffodils with late-emerging, sturdy perennials such as hosta, grasses or daylilies.

sources.title: Purdue Extension: Gardening with Bulbs

companions.why: Purdue Extension: plant tulips with later-emerging plants that hide the ripening foliage, especially hosta, daylily and ornamental grasses.

sources.title: Purdue Extension: Gardening with Bulbs

companions.why: Pair with fall aster, bugbane, eupatorium, goldenrod, sedum or toad lily; near bleeding heart; with variegated hosta and grasses.

companions.why: A border is brightened when obedient plant is planted alongside goldenrods, little bluestem and purple coneflower.

sources.title: Mt. Cuba Center: Obedient Plant

companions.why: Combined with fall-blooming sedums; a great filler between purple coneflower, liatris, black-eyed Susan and butterfly weed.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Prairie Dropseed article

companions.why: Grows well with blazing star and little bluestem; often grows with prairie dropseed in natural settings.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Prairie Smoke article

companions.why: Combines well with other prairie plants, such as Liatris and little bluestem.

companions.why: Combines well with ornamental grasses, anise hyssop, beebalm, daylilies, fall asters, liatris, purple coneflower and rudbeckias.
